extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers interested in the history and practice of 18th-century newspaper advertising
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter excerpt surveying mid-18th-century newspaper advertisements and contemporary critical commentary (notably Dr. Johnson) about advertising style, techniques, conventions, and social effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promise, large promise, is the soul of an advertisement
rubrics_metrics.description: "Promise, large promise, is the soul of an advertisement." (Dr. Johnson) — assertion that bold promises are central to effective adverts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gain attention by making magnified promises; examples include sensational claims for washballs, duvets 'warmer than four or five blankets', and lotions that 'repel pimples' or 'smooth the skin'. Use of sublime or pathetic eloquence may be effective. Beware of overreach—claims should be persuasive but not wholly incredible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gain attention by magnificence of promises and eloquence
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements should 'gain attention by magnificence of promises, and by eloquence sometimes sublime and sometimes pathetic.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ grand or emotive language where appropriate to attract readers' eye. Dr. Johnson illustrates this with extravagant product claims; this technique is effective for crowded pages where ordinary notices are neglected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use independent testimony or quotation to bolster credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoting independent authorities or testimonials (e.g., widow Gatesfield quoting a poem/testimony about a maker) to support claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include endorsements, literary references, or quotations as evidence of quality. Example: citing a recognized name or poem to intimate lineage or skill. This increases perceived legitimacy and helps sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide tangible proofs or receipts when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Vendors claiming quality should be willing to 'produce receipts in a court of justice' or other proofs (John Ward's claim).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer verifiable evidence (receipts, testimonials, past orders) to counter accusations of deceit and to reassure purchasers; stating willingness to produce proof increases trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gratuitous attacks on competitors; privilege self-praise not neighbour-censure
rubrics_metrics.description: In an advertisement 'it is allowed to every man to speak well of himself, but ... he should not assume the privilege of censuring his neighbour.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame adverts positively about your own goods/services rather than attacking rivals. Personal asperity and bitter disputes in print reflect poorly and can reduce credibility (examples: disputes about strops, Eau de Luce).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider dignity and posterity when composing adverts
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisers should 'write with some consciousness of a character which dares to call the attention of the public' and remember that papers may be collected for posterity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use decorous language and avoid content that will look foolish to future readers; treat your printed statement as lasting record—this supports reputation management and long-term credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper disposition and juxtaposition of advertisements
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful how adverts are placed and associated: improper disposition can make even noble objects 'ridiculous' (Dr. Johnson's warning about juxtaposition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid placing exalted or solemn notices immediately adjacent to trivial or bawdy adverts. Editorial/layout considerations (classification/separation) matter to how an ad's tone will be perceived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classified, regularly formatted advertising pages create a modern look
rubrics_metrics.description: The General Advertiser introduced columns 'filled with them, between fifty and sixty, regularly classified and separated by rules' giving a modern appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use consistent classification and separation (rules/columns) so readers can find specific kinds of notices. A predictable, tidy layout increases readability and perceived professionalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of illustrations/engravings to attract attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclusion of 'finely engraved' prints (dreams, ships, ticket fruits) as part of adverts to entice readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ images or engravings where possible to make an advertisement stand out in the column and to visually represent the product or novelty being sold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about target audience and eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Many personal or matrimonial notices specifically state eligibility (e.g., 'If a single woman', 'if unmarried', 'Any Person who shall send a Letter...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly indicate who should respond and any conditions (e.g., single, unmarried). This reduces irrelevant replies and signals seriousness of the offer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promise and protect confidentiality where required
rubrics_metrics.description: Matchmaking/introductory adverts commonly promise 'Secrecy and Honour will be observed' when bringing persons together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer assurances of discretion in sensitive ads (matrimonial, scandal-sensitive matters). Explicit promises of secrecy can increase response from cautious correspondents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use letters-to-editor / personal-letter forms as effective ad format
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisers often framed notices as letters or testimonials (e.g., Elizabeth Gardiner's letter praising a staymaker) to promote services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a first-person or testimonial letter format to create a personal tone and social proof; this can read as an independent endorsement even when authored by the seller or an associate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include clear contact and transactional details (where/how to apply)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ads provide precise instructions for contact (where to leave letters, named coffee-houses, times, places) and service particulars (methods to apply, salaries, fees).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give precise instructions (addresses, drop-off locations, times) and describe exactly what the advertiser offers or arranges (vacancies, methods). Clear logistics increase the likelihood of successful responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of promotional devices (lotteries, guaranteed prizes) to entice customers
rubrics_metrics.description: Promotional gimmicks such as 'A Lottery For Husbands... Not one Blank, but All Prizes' were used to attract buyers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ lotteries, guaranteed prizes, or similar enticements to stimulate interest and sales; make terms explicit (classes of tickets, prizes) to persuade purchase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe legal and regulatory constraints on ad wording
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory restrictions affected advertising language (e.g., an Act forbade notification of 'no questions asked' in lost/stolen property adverts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure adverts comply with current laws and statutes governing permitted language and promises; avoid wording (like 'no questions asked') that legal rules prohibit or that attract penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modest admissions of limitation can increase credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Sellers sometimes candidly admitted limitations (e.g., a lotion 'will not restore the bloom of fifteen to a lady of fifty'), which appealed to public taste for 'modest sincerity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategic modesty—acknowledging realistic limits—can make other claims seem more trustworthy. Use measured honesty to counteract incredulity from overblown promises.
